questions.q: Why can't a standard UI Policy (from Course 2) control a catalog variable?
options: Standard UI Policies can control variables; Catalog UI Policies are optional
Catalog variables live in item_option_new/sc_item_option, not as columns on the form's underlying table, so the standard UI Policy engine has no way to see or react to them
Variables cannot be shown or hidden at all
Standard UI Policies only work on mobile devices
questions.explain: Catalog variables are a fundamentally different structure from table fields, which is exactly why ServiceNow built a separate catalog_ui_policy object type.

questions.q: Which three actions can a Catalog UI Policy apply to a target variable?
options: Visible, Mandatory, Read-only
Create, Update, Delete
Approve, Reject, Escalate
Public, Private, Hidden
questions.explain: These are the same three levers as a standard UI Policy, just aimed at catalog variables instead of table fields.

questions.q: In the worked example, what does the Catalog UI Policy do when "Cost Center Override" is checked?
options: It deletes the catalog item
It submits the request automatically
It makes "Manager Approval Reason" visible and mandatory, where it was previously hidden and not required
It changes the catalog item's price
questions.explain: The condition (Cost Center Override = true) drives the action: the Manager Approval Reason variable becomes both visible and mandatory.

questions.q: Where does a Catalog UI Policy run, and what does that mean for the requester's experience?
options: On the server only, requiring a full page reload for every change
It does not run until the request is approved
It runs once per day via a scheduled job
On the client, so the form reacts live and instantly as the requester fills it in, with no page reload
questions.explain: Like standard UI Policies, Catalog UI Policies are client-side — the show/hide/mandatory behavior happens live in the browser.

questions.q: What's the common early mistake this lesson warns against?
options: Building a Catalog UI Policy expecting it to control a real table field, or looking for a catalog variable in the regular UI Policy list — because the two object types act on different kinds of data
Forgetting to price a catalog item
Using too many variable types on one catalog item
Assigning a catalog item to the wrong category
questions.explain: Knowing up front whether you need a standard UI Policy or a Catalog UI Policy avoids troubleshooting a rule that looks correct but was built against the wrong object type.
